queries: Madam Vinous sweet orange seedlings are widely recognized as an excellent indicator plant for the detection of citrus viruses and viroids, particularly under warm greenhouse conditions. The warm environment accelerates plant growth and symptom expression, making it easier to observe characteristic disease indicators. When infected with specific pathogens, such as citrus tristeza virus or certain viroids, these seedlings exhibit distinct leaf symptoms, including chlorosis, vein clearing, and stunting, which are reliable visual markers for diagnosis. The sensitivity of Madam Vinous to these pathogens is attributed to its genetic susceptibility and rapid physiological response under elevated temperatures. Additionally, the uniform growth habit of these seedlings ensures consistent and reproducible results across experiments, which is critical for accurate pathogen indexing. The warm greenhouse conditions also reduce the incubation period, allowing for faster detection and more efficient screening of infected plant material. This combination of high sensitivity, clear symptom development, and rapid response makes Madam Vinous sweet orange seedlings a preferred bioassay tool in citrus pathology research and quarantine programs. Furthermore, the ease of propagation and maintenance of these seedlings under controlled greenhouse environments enhances their practicality as an indicator host. Overall, the use of Madam Vinous sweet orange seedlings under warm conditions provides a reliable, cost-effective, and time-efficient method for the early detection and identification of citrus pathogens, supporting both research and regulatory efforts.

## Abstract

## 2.1 Plant material  
Nicotiana benthamiana seedlings were maintained in a growth chamber at 25circ C with a 16/8 h light/dark photoperiod. Agrobacterium tumefaciens infiltration was conducted on N. benthamiana leaves at the four- to six-leaf stage. Two-year-old sweet orange was used as a rootstock to propagate the obtained RNAi-CsERF1 transgenic plants. One-year-old healthy sweet orange seedlings (Madam virons) were treated with exogenous hormones, and plants used in tissue-specific experiments were 5-year-old healthy sweet orange seedlings and sweet orange seedlings infected with CTV, which were stored in the greenhouse of Citrus Research Institute of Southwest University for future use.

The bio-indicators were placed in cool (20-22ºC) and warm (28-32ºC) insect-proof glasshouse rooms and observed periodically for virus and viroid symptom expression. Seven to 10 weeks post-inoculation, tissue samples from the indicators were collected for ELISA tests for CTLV (polyclonal Loewe) and CPsV (monoclonal Agritest) and RT-PCR using newly designed and published primers (1, 8, 12).

## Virus detection  
Virus detection was carried out in various citrus tissues and organs, including leaves, fruit peels, undeveloped ovules, and embryoids. Specifically, virus detection was carried out in fruit peels and leaves from ZC and LL leaves from Newhall Navel orange, Hamlin orange, Early Gold sweet orange, Valencia sweet orange, Red Tangerine, Blood orange, Bendizao tangerine, and Ponkan. All regenerated plant scions, as well as undeveloped ovules and embryoids during tissue culture, were also assessed for virus presence. Total RNA was extracted from all these materials using a kit (Aidlab Biotechnology, Beijing, China) following the manufacturer's instructions. cDNA was synthesized using HiScript II Q RT SuperMix for qPCR (+gDNA wiper; Vazyme, Nanjing, China).
